subject: Civil Engineering
title: Road Geometry: Curves and Grades
description: A quick win: understand Road Geometry: Curves and Grades.

hook.text: A sharp curve at highway speed is deadly. The road's shape keeps you alive.

buildup.text: Horizontal curves are arcs. Vertical curves crest over hills or dip through valleys.

discovery.text: Superelevation banks the road on curves — tilting it so gravity helps you turn.

twist.text: Too steep a grade and trucks crawl. Too flat and water pools on the surface.

climax.text: Every curve radius, grade, and sight distance follows strict design standards.

punchline.text: Roads aren't just paved paths — they're engineered geometry.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of superelevation on a road curve?
options: It makes the road look more appealing to drivers
It banks the road to help vehicles turn safely using gravity
It increases the speed limit on curved sections

details.summary: Road geometry defines the three-dimensional alignment of a highway through horizontal curves, vertical grades, and superelevation. Engineers design curves with adequate radius and banking so vehicles can safely navigate at design speed.
details.whyItMatters: Geometric design directly determines road safety. Inadequate curve radius or insufficient sight distance over hills are leading causes of fatal single-vehicle crashes on rural highways.
takeaways: Horizontal curve radius depends on design speed and superelevation rate
Vertical curves are parabolas connecting tangent grades for smooth transitions
Stopping sight distance must be maintained over every crest vertical curve

faq.question: What is superelevation and why do curves need it?
faq.answer: Superelevation tilts the road surface toward the inside of a curve, using gravity to help counteract centrifugal force. Without it, vehicles at design speed would need friction alone to stay on the road. Maximum superelevation is typically 8-12% depending on climate conditions.

faq.question: How do engineers design vertical curves over hills?
faq.answer: Crest vertical curves must be long enough that a driver at the summit can see a stopped vehicle ahead within stopping distance. The required curve length depends on design speed, driver eye height, and object height. Higher speeds require much longer, gentler curves.
